Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

The map
$$\Phi:\mathbb C\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2,\qquad \Phi(a+bi)=(a,b),$$
is a bijection. Under it,
$$\Phi((a+bi)+(u+vi))=(a+u,b+v)$$
and
$$\Phi((a+bi)(u+vi))=(au-bv,av+bu).$$

For an endomorphism $T$ of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, the following are equivalent:

1. $T$ preserves norms.
2. $T$ preserves inner products.
3. $T$ sends every orthonormal basis to an orthonormal basis.
4. $T$ sends some orthonormal basis to an orthonormal basis.
5. $T^*T=I$.

Whenever these conditions hold, $T$ is invertible and $T^{-1}=T^*$, so also $TT^*=I$. The zero-dimensional case is included.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Matrix multiplication over a field is associative and unital, distributes over
entrywise addition on both sides, and is compatible with scalar multiplication.
Precisely, whenever the displayed products have compatible shapes,

$$A(BC)=(AB)C,\qquad I_mA=A=AI_n,$$

$$(A+A')B=AB+A'B,\qquad A(B+B')=AB+AB',$$

$$0B=0=A0,\qquad (\lambda A)B=\lambda(AB)=A(\lambda B).$$

These identities include every zero-sized shape.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- An **open cover** of $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is a family
  $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ of open sets with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$,
  where $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$
  that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \varnothing$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite
  subcover: for every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \varnothing$ and the
  empty subfamily covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the subspace
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is a compact topological space, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the
  subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ and its own open
sets, not about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do
agree, but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], and no item of this library may use
the ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading makes
compactness a property of the topological space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ alone.
Hence it is preserved when $A$ is embedded homeomorphically as a subspace, or
when another ambient space induces the same topology on $A$; it need not be
preserved if the induced topology changes. This is exactly the convention already fixed for
metric spaces by [[def-metric-compactness]], and the agreement of that
definition with this one is [[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]].

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. Every
space listed as $\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ is compact too: given a cover, each $x_i$
lies in some member, and finitely many members named in this way already cover.
So every finite space is compact, whatever its topology, and in particular the
discrete topology on a finite set is compact while the discrete topology on an
infinite set is not ([[def-standard-topologies]]).

**The finiteness convention.** "Finite" above is the listing form. It agrees with
the definition of finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number
([[def-countable]]), in both directions, and the agreement is the one already
discharged in [[def-metric-compactness]]: a nonempty set equinumerous with
$m \ge 1$ is listable, and a set listed as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$ injects into
$\sigma(n)$ by sending $x$ to the least $i \le n$ with $a_i = x$. Neither
direction uses a choice principle; the second selects nothing, taking a least
index instead.

**Quasicompact is not used here.** Some authors, following Bourbaki, reserve
*compact* for a space that is both compact in the above sense and Hausdorff, and
call the open-cover condition alone *quasicompact*. This library follows the more
widely adopted convention: **compact** means the open-cover condition and nothing
more, and a Hausdorff hypothesis is always written out. The fork is recorded in
[[rem-compactness-conventions-and-choice-ledger]].

A topological space $(X, \mathcal{T})$ ([[def-topological-space]]) is
**Hausdorff** when any two distinct points are separated by disjoint open sets:
for all $x, y \in X$ with $x \ne y$ there are $U, V \in \mathcal{T}$ with

$$x \in U, \qquad y \in V, \qquad U \cap V = \varnothing .$$

Since an open set containing a point is an open neighbourhood of it
([[def-neighbourhood-top]]), the condition reads: distinct points have disjoint
open neighbourhoods. Nothing is asserted about points that are equal, and the
condition is vacuous for a space with at most one point, so every such space is
Hausdorff.

**Every metrizable space is Hausdorff.** This is not proved here, because it is
already discharged: [[def-metrizable-space]] records it among the two things
every metrizable space has, deriving it from
[[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]], which separates $p \ne q$ in a metric space
by the disjoint open balls $B(p,r)$ and $B(q,r)$ with $r = d(p,q)/2 > 0$. In
particular $\mathbb{R}$ with its usual topology, every $\mathbb{R}^n$, and every
subspace of a metrizable space are Hausdorff.

**Not every space is Hausdorff.** The indiscrete topology
$\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ind}} = \{\varnothing, X\}$ on a set $X = \{a,b\}$ with
$a \ne b$ ([[def-standard-topologies]]) is not: the only open set containing $a$
is $X$, the only one containing $b$ is $X$, and $X \cap X = X \ne \varnothing$.
This is the same two-point space that [[def-metrizable-space]] uses to exhibit a
topology induced by no metric, and the reason is the same one: failure of the
Hausdorff condition is an obstruction to metrizability.

**Being Hausdorff is a topological property** ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).
If $h : X \to Z$ is a homeomorphism and $X$ is Hausdorff, then for $z \ne z'$ in
$Z$ the points $h^{-1}(z)$ and $h^{-1}(z')$ are distinct, so they have disjoint
open $U, V$; the images $h[U]$ and $h[V]$ are open, disjoint, and contain $z$ and
$z'$ respectively, a homeomorphism carrying the open sets of one space
bijectively onto those of the other. So no space homeomorphic to a Hausdorff
space fails the condition.

**Scope of this item.** Only the definition, the metrizable case and the
two-point failure are recorded here, because that is all this page uses. The
Hausdorff condition is one of a graded family of separation axioms; that family,
its ordering, and the questions of which of its members are hereditary or
preserved by products, are not available at this point in the reading order and
nothing here anticipates them. What this page does use is a single negative
result: a quotient of a Hausdorff space need not be Hausdorff, which is recorded
below as a false statement and witnessed on the companion page.

A **topological group** is a group $G$ ([[def-group]]) with a topology such that multiplication $m:G\times G\to G$, $m(x,y)=xy$, and inversion $\iota:G\to G$, $\iota(x)=x^{-1}$, are continuous ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) for the product topology ([[def-product-topology]]).

A **group** is a monoid $(G,*,e)$ ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]) in which every
element is invertible ([[def-invertible-element]]). Written out, a group is a set
$G$ with a binary operation $*$ ([[def-binary-operation]]) and an element
$e \in G$ such that

- **(G1)** $(x * y) * z = x * (y * z)$ for all $x, y, z \in G$;
- **(G2)** $e * x = x = x * e$ for every $x \in G$;
- **(G3)** for every $x \in G$ there is $y \in G$ with $y * x = e = x * y$.

By [[lem-identity-unique]] the element $e$ of (G2) is unique, and by
[[lem-inverse-unique]] the element $y$ of (G3) is unique for each $x$ and is
determined by either one of the two equations alone. So the notations $e$ for the
identity and $x^{-1}$ for the inverse of $x$ are legitimate, and asserting
$y * x = e$ alone already says $y = x^{-1}$.

A group is **abelian**, or **commutative**, when its operation is commutative:
$x * y = y * x$ for all $x, y \in G$.

**Notation.** The operation is usually written multiplicatively, $xy$ for
$x * y$, with identity $e$ (or $1$) and inverse $x^{-1}$. For an abelian group it
is often written additively, $x + y$, with identity $0$ and inverse $-x$; the two
notations describe the same notion and nothing below depends on the choice. We
write $G$ for the group when the operation is understood.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $\mathcal{T}_d$ be
its metric topology ([[def-metric-topology]]), so that $(X, \mathcal{T}_d)$ is a
topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and is metrizable
([[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. $(X,d)$ is a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]) **if and only
   if** $(X, \mathcal{T}_d)$ is a compact topological space
   ([[def-compact-space]]).
2. For every $A \subseteq X$: $A$ is a compact subset of the metric space
   $(X,d)$ if and only if $A$ is a compact subset of the topological space
   $(X, \mathcal{T}_d)$, the two readings of "compact subset" being the metric
   subspace $(A, d_A)$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]) and the topological
   subspace $(A, (\mathcal{T}_d)_A)$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Nothing here is a coincidence and nothing is transported.** The open-cover
condition of [[def-metric-compactness]] quantifies over families of subsets open
in $(X,d)$, and by [[def-metric-topology]] those are exactly the members of
$\mathcal{T}_d$; so the two conditions are not merely equivalent, they are the
same condition written twice. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: The map $U\mapsto U^*U$ is continuous because each entry is a finite sum of products of real-coordinate polynomial expressions from [F2]. The singleton $\{I_d\}$ is closed in the finite-dimensional Euclidean matrix space, so its inverse image $U(d)$ is closed. If $U=(u_{ij})\in U(d)$, each column has squared Euclidean norm $\sum_i|u_{ij}|^2=1$; hence every real and imaginary entry lies in $[-1,1]$. Thus $U(d)$ is bounded in $\mathbb R^{2d^2}$.

By Heine–Borel and the agreement of metric and topological compactness in [F1], the closed bounded set $U(d)$ from step 1.1 is compact in its Euclidean subspace topology. Distinct points of $U(d)$ have disjoint sufficiently small Euclidean balls, so its subspace topology is Hausdorff by [F5]. It is nonempty because $I_d\in U(d)$.

By [F3], each $U\in U(d)$ has inverse $U^*$, so the defining set is closed under inverses. If $U,V\in U(d)$, then $(UV)^*(UV)=V^*(U^*U)V=V^*V=I_d$, so it is closed under multiplication; associativity and the identity follow from [F4]. Matrix multiplication is continuous by the finite coordinate formulas of step 1.1, and inversion is $U\mapsto U^*$, which is continuous by [F2]. Thus the group with its subspace topology is a topological group by [F5].

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

derivations.claim: Diagonalize $X$ and let $M\ge0$ be its largest eigenvalue; if $X=0$, take $M=0$. Diagonalize $\sigma$ and let $m>0$ be its smallest eigenvalue, which is positive by faithfulness and [F2]. For every $v\in H$, these spectral bounds give $\langle Xv,v\rangle\le M\|v\|^2$ and $\langle\sigma v,v\rangle\ge m\|v\|^2$.

Set $c=M/m$. Then $c$ is finite and nonnegative, and for every $v$ step 1.1 gives $\langle(c\sigma-X)v,v\rangle\ge (cm-M)\|v\|^2=0$. By [F3], $c\sigma-X\ge0$, which is exactly $X\le c\sigma$. This also covers $X=0$ with $c=0$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $\rho,\sigma$ be density operators on $H$ (nonnegative operators of trace one; [[def-qc-density-operator]]). Their **root fidelity** is
$$F(\rho,\sigma):=\|\sqrt\rho\,\sqrt\sigma\|_1,$$
where $\sqrt\rho$ and $\sqrt\sigma$ are the unique non-negative square roots and $\|\cdot\|_1$ is the finite-dimensional trace norm ([[def-qc-trace-norm]]). This library uses root fidelity; the squared quantity $F(\rho,\sigma)^2$ is called squared fidelity.

Let $A:H\to K$ be a linear map ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces. Its singular values are the eigenvalues of
$|A|:=\sqrt{A^*A}:H\to H$, counted with multiplicity, as defined in
[[def-singular-values-of-an-endomorphism]]. Define the **trace norm**, or
Schatten-$1$ norm, by

$$\|A\|_1:=\sum_{j<\dim H}s_j(A).$$

The sum includes zero singular values and is $0$ when $H$ is the zero space.
For this definition, $A$ may be rectangular; the singular values are those of
$|A|$ on the domain $H$. The spectral trace formula is proved in
[[thm-qc-trace-norm-spectral-formula]].

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

derivations.claim: Put $A=\sqrt\rho\sqrt\sigma$. Since $A^*=\sqrt\sigma\sqrt\rho$, we have $A^*A=\sqrt\sigma\,\rho\,\sqrt\sigma$ and $AA^*=\sqrt\rho\,\sigma\,\sqrt\rho$. Both are non-negative. By [L1], the eigenvalues of $A^*A$ and $AA^*$ are the squares of the singular values of $A$; because $A$ is an endomorphism, the SVD lists the same $d$ singular values on both sides, with zero multiplicity included.

The unique non-negative square roots of $A^*A$ and $AA^*$ therefore have the same eigenvalue list, namely the singular values of $A$. Their traces both equal the sum of those singular values, which is $\|A\|_1$ by [L1]. Substituting $AA^*=\sqrt\rho\,\sigma\,\sqrt\rho$ proves the stated identity and, by [F1], its equivalent root-fidelity expression.

Let $A:H\to K$ be a linear map ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces. Its singular values are the eigenvalues of
$|A|:=\sqrt{A^*A}:H\to H$, counted with multiplicity, as defined in
[[def-singular-values-of-an-endomorphism]]. Define the **trace norm**, or
Schatten-$1$ norm, by

$$\|A\|_1:=\sum_{j<\dim H}s_j(A).$$

The sum includes zero singular values and is $0$ when $H$ is the zero space.
For this definition, $A$ may be rectangular; the singular values are those of
$|A|$ on the domain $H$. The spectral trace formula is proved in
[[thm-qc-trace-norm-spectral-formula]].

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

derivations.claim: If either $A$ or $B$ is zero, or a domain or codomain factor is zero-dimensional, then $A\otimes B=0$ and at least one factor trace norm is zero, so the formula holds. Otherwise choose SVDs $A z=\sum_{i=1}^r s_i\langle z,v_i\rangle u_i$ and $B w=\sum_{j=1}^q t_j\langle w,q_j\rangle p_j$ as in [F2], with all $s_i,t_j>0$.

By [F3], on elementary tensors $$ (A\otimes B)(z\otimes w)=\sum_{i=1}^r\sum_{j=1}^q s_it_j\langle z\otimes w,v_i\otimes q_j\rangle\,u_i\otimes p_j.$$ The families $(v_i\otimes q_j)_{i,j}$ and $(u_i\otimes p_j)_{i,j}$ are orthonormal because their pairings are products of the factor pairings. Since elementary tensors span, this is a singular-value decomposition of $A\otimes B$ with positive singular values exactly $s_it_j$. Thus [F1] gives $$\|A\otimes B\|_1=\sum_{i,j}s_it_j=\left(\sum_i s_i\right)\left(\sum_jt_j\right)=\|A\|_1\|B\|_1.$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. The orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]]) gives

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp$$

and associates to every $v\in V$ unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$. The **orthogonal projection onto $W$** is the function

$$P_W:V\longrightarrow W,\qquad P_Wv=w.$$

Equivalently, $P_Wv$ is the unique vector of $W$ such that $v-P_Wv\in W^\perp$.

Let $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ be an orthonormal basis of a subspace $W$ of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. Then

$$P_Wv=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle e_i.$$

The map $P_W$ is linear, with image $W$, kernel $W^\perp$, and $P_W^2=P_W$. Moreover, regarding both projections as endomorphisms of $V$,

$$I-P_W=P_{W^\perp}.$$

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

Let $(T_k:H_k\to K_k)_{k<n}$ and $(S_k:K_k\to L_k)_{k<n}$ be finite ordered
families of linear maps between finite-dimensional complex inner-product
spaces. Then

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}S_k\right)\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)=\bigotimes_{k<n}(S_kT_k),\qquad \bigotimes_{k<n}I_{H_k}=I_{\otimes_{k<n}H_k},\qquad \left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)^*=\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k^*.$$

In the first formula, $S_kT_k$ means $S_k\circ T_k$. Here $I_{H_k}$ denotes
the identity map $x\mapsto x$. All adjoints use the
repository pairing, linear in the first argument. The empty tensor-map
identity is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on $\mathbb C$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

derivations.claim: Let $Q=I-P_S$. By [F1], the range of $\operatorname{Tr}_2Y$ lies in $S$, so $Q\operatorname{Tr}_2Y=0$ and $\operatorname{tr}(Q\operatorname{Tr}_2Y)=0$. By [L1], $\operatorname{tr}((Q\otimes I)Y)=0$. Cyclicity of trace rewrites this as $\operatorname{tr}(Y^{1/2}(Q\otimes I)Y^{1/2})=0$. Since [L2] gives $(Q\otimes I)^*=(Q\otimes I)^2=Q\otimes I$, the operator inside the trace is $Z^*Z\ge0$ for $Z=(Q\otimes I)Y^{1/2}$; [F2] makes it zero, hence $Z=0$ because $\langle Z^*Zv,v\rangle=\|Zv\|^2$. Thus $(Q\otimes I)Y=Y(Q\otimes I)=0$, and $Y=(P_S\otimes I)Y(P_S\otimes I)$.
Applying the same argument to the second marginal with the projection $I\otimes Q$ gives $Y=(I\otimes P_S)Y(I\otimes P_S)$.

The two commuting projections $P_S\otimes I$ and $I\otimes P_S$ have product $P_S\otimes P_S$ by [L3]. Combining step 1.1 and step 2.1 yields $Y=(P_S\otimes P_S)Y(P_S\otimes P_S)$, so the range and hence the support of $Y$ lies in $S\otimes S$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $\rho,\sigma$ be density operators on $H$ (nonnegative operators of trace one; [[def-qc-density-operator]]). Their **trace distance** is
$$D(\rho,\sigma):=\tfrac12\|\rho-\sigma\|_1,$$
where $\|\cdot\|_1$ is the trace norm ([[def-qc-trace-norm]]). The factor $1/2$ is part of this state-distance convention. The diamond norm below is an unhalved norm on maps.

Let $\mathcal H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let
$X:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H$ be self-adjoint. There are non-negative
endomorphisms $X_+,X_-$ such that

$$X=X_+-X_-,\qquad \langle X_+u,X_-v\rangle=0\quad(u,v\in\mathcal H),$$

and

$$\|X\|_1=\operatorname{tr}(X_+)+\operatorname{tr}(X_-).$$

If $\operatorname{tr}(X)=0$, then
$\|X\|_1=2\operatorname{tr}(X_+)=2\operatorname{tr}(X_-)$. 

The trace norm is the finite singular-value norm from
[[def-qc-trace-norm]].

derivations.claim: Put $c=|\langle u|v\rangle_D|\in[0,1]$ by [F2] and the unit norms. If $c=1$, equality in [F2] makes $v$ a unit scalar multiple of $u$, so $P_u=P_v$ and both sides are zero. Suppose $c<1$. Multiplying $v$ by a unit scalar does not change $P_v$ and lets us assume $\langle v,u\rangle_{\rm root}=c$: if $a=\langle v,u\rangle_{\rm root}\ne0$, multiply $v$ by $\overline a/|a|$. Define $w=(v-cu)/\sqrt{1-c^2}$. Direct expansion using [F1] gives $\langle w,u\rangle_{\rm root}=0$ and $\|w\|=1$, so $(u,w)$ is orthonormal and $v=cu+\sqrt{1-c^2}w$.

In the orthonormal basis $(u,w)$ of their span, $P_u-P_v$ has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1-c^2&-c\sqrt{1-c^2}\\-c\sqrt{1-c^2}&-(1-c^2)\end{pmatrix}$. Its trace is zero and determinant is $-(1-c^2)$, so its two eigenvalues are $\sqrt{1-c^2}$ and $-\sqrt{1-c^2}$; it is zero on the orthogonal complement. By [L2], $\|P_u-P_v\|_1=2\sqrt{1-c^2}$.

order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

derivations.claim: For $k\ge1$, $\Pi^*=\frac1{k!}\sum_\pi U_\pi^*=\frac1{k!}\sum_\pi U_{\pi^{-1}}=\Pi$ by [L1] and reindexing by inversion. For every $\tau\in S_k$, $U_\tau\Pi=\frac1{k!}\sum_\pi U_{\pi\circ\tau}=\Pi$ by [L1] and reindexing by right multiplication. Hence every vector in $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$ is invariant. Conversely, if $U_\pi v=v$ for all $\pi$, then $\Pi v=\frac1{k!}\sum_\pi v=v$. Therefore $\operatorname{ran}\Pi=\operatorname{Sym}^k(H)$.

Let $A:H\to K$ be a linear map ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces. Its singular values are the eigenvalues of
$|A|:=\sqrt{A^*A}:H\to H$, counted with multiplicity, as defined in
[[def-singular-values-of-an-endomorphism]]. Define the **trace norm**, or
Schatten-$1$ norm, by

$$\|A\|_1:=\sum_{j<\dim H}s_j(A).$$

The sum includes zero singular values and is $0$ when $H$ is the zero space.
For this definition, $A$ may be rectangular; the singular values are those of
$|A|$ on the domain $H$. The spectral trace formula is proved in
[[thm-qc-trace-norm-spectral-formula]].

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Let $(T_k:H_k\to K_k)_{k<n}$ and $(S_k:K_k\to L_k)_{k<n}$ be finite ordered
families of linear maps between finite-dimensional complex inner-product
spaces. Then

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}S_k\right)\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)=\bigotimes_{k<n}(S_kT_k),\qquad \bigotimes_{k<n}I_{H_k}=I_{\otimes_{k<n}H_k},\qquad \left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)^*=\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k^*.$$

In the first formula, $S_kT_k$ means $S_k\circ T_k$. Here $I_{H_k}$ denotes
the identity map $x\mapsto x$. All adjoints use the
repository pairing, linear in the first argument. The empty tensor-map
identity is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on $\mathbb C$.

Let $H,H'$ be finite-dimensional (have finite bases by [[def-dimension]])
complex inner-product spaces with ordered
orthonormal bases $(e_u)_{u<n}$ and $(f_s)_{s<m}$. For $u,v<n$ and $s,t<m$
define $E_{uv}x:=\langle x,e_v\rangle e_u$ and
$F_{st}y:=\langle y,f_t\rangle f_s$. Then
$(E_{uv}\otimes F_{st})_{u,v,s,t}$ is a basis of
$\mathcal L(H\otimes H')$. Empty dimensions give the empty basis of the zero
endomorphism space. The root pairing is linear in its first argument, so the
displayed matrix-unit maps are linear.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex-inner-product spaces with the tensor-product convention of [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]]. For every $\Psi\in H\otimes K$ there are an integer $r\ge0$, positive numbers $s_1,\ldots,s_r$, and orthonormal families $u_1,\ldots,u_r\in H$ and $v_1,\ldots,v_r\in K$ such that

$$\Psi=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j u_j\otimes v_j,\qquad \|\Psi\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j^2.$$

For $\Psi=0$ take $r=0$ and the empty sum. For any chosen ordered pair of orthonormal bases, the construction below obtains the $s_j$ as the positive singular values of the coefficient matrix of $\Psi$ in their ordered product basis.

Let $A:H\to K$ be a linear map ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional complex
inner-product spaces. Then

$$\|A\|_1=\max\{\,|\operatorname{tr}_H(B^*A)|: B:H\to K\text{ linear and }\|B\|\le1\,\}.$$

Consequently, on the vector space of linear maps $H\to K$, the trace norm is
nonnegative, absolutely homogeneous, definite, and satisfies the triangle
inequality.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

derivations.claim: For fixed $r$, let $M_r$ be the maximum of $\|(\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_r)(R_{u,v})\|_1$ over unit vectors $u,v\in H\otimes\mathbb C^r$. Their unit spheres are compact by [F1]. In orthonormal coordinates each entry of $R_{u,v}$ is a finite product of coordinates of $u$ and conjugates of coordinates of $v$; applying the finite linear map $\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_r$ remains continuous, and [L4] makes the output trace norm continuous. Hence the maximum exists. By [L1], every $X$ with $\|X\|_1\le1$ has an SVD $X=\sum_js_jR_{u_j,v_j}$ with unit $u_j,v_j$, $s_j\ge0$, and $\sum_js_j\le1$. Linearity and the trace-norm triangle inequality give $\|(\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_r)(X)\|_1\le\sum_js_jM_r\le M_r$. For unit $u,v$, the adjoint calculation gives $R_{u,v}^*R_{u,v}=R_{v,v}$, a rank-one orthogonal projection, so its singular values are one $1$ and the remaining zeros; hence $\|R_{u,v}\|_1=1$. Thus the induced norm equals $M_r$ and is attained.

Now take any finite ancilla $Z$ and unit vectors $x,y\in H\otimes Z$. By [L3], their Schmidt ranks $a,b$ are at most $\min(d,\dim Z)$. Let $m=\max(a,b)$ and pad each Schmidt list to an orthonormal $m$-tuple, obtaining $x',y'\in H\otimes\mathbb C^m$. The tensor-map definition and product pairing show each map $I\otimes V_x$ and $I\otimes V_y$ is an isometry. Factor permutations are unitary because they carry an orthonormal product basis bijectively to another such basis. Thus $$(\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_Z)(R_{x,y})=(I_K\otimes V_x)(\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_m)(R_{x',y'})(I_K\otimes V_y)^*.$$ To verify the equality, expand operators in elementary tensors $A\otimes B$: $\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}$ sends this to $\Phi(A)\otimes B$, and the two isometries send each ancilla matrix unit $R_{e_i,e_j}$ to $R_{z_i,w_j}$. For isometries $U,V$, $(UA_0V^*)^*(UA_0V^*)=VA_0^*A_0V^*$. The positive eigenvalues of this operator are those of $A_0^*A_0$: an eigenvector $z$ with positive eigenvalue maps to $Vz$, and any eigenvector with positive eigenvalue must lie in the range of $V$ because the operator vanishes on its orthogonal complement. Hence left/right isometric embeddings preserve the nonzero singular values and trace norm. Embedding $\mathbb C^m$ isometrically into $\mathbb C^d$ on both sides is the same case, so the original output has trace norm at most $\|\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_d\|_{1\to1}$.

By step 1.1, the induced norm for each $Z$ is attained by a rank-one unit input, so step 1.2 gives $\|\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_Z\|_{1\to1}\le\|\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_d\|_{1\to1}$. Taking the supremum over all finite $Z$ gives $\|\Phi\|_\diamond\le\|\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_d\|_{1\to1}$. The reverse inequality holds because $r=d$ is one of the ancilla dimensions in the supremum. Step 1.1 at $r=d$ supplies an attaining rank-one operator.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $\rho,\sigma$ be density operators on $H$ (nonnegative operators of trace one; [[def-qc-density-operator]]). Their **trace distance** is
$$D(\rho,\sigma):=\tfrac12\|\rho-\sigma\|_1,$$
where $\|\cdot\|_1$ is the trace norm ([[def-qc-trace-norm]]). The factor $1/2$ is part of this state-distance convention. The diamond norm below is an unhalved norm on maps.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space; the pairing is linear in its first argument ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for its complex-linear endomorphisms ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]) and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite POVM** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $E=(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ with each $E_a$ nonnegative and $\sum_{a\in\Omega}E_a=I_H$; after any enumeration of $\Omega$, these operators form the finite complete positive family of [[def-qc-finite-positive-effect-family]]. Reordering does not alter the finite sum. The complete-family lemma [[lem-qc-complete-effect-family-members-are-effects]] shows that every $E_a$ also has nonnegative complement $I_H-E_a$, so each is an effect.

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (a nonnegative operator of trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), its **POVM outcome weights** are

$$p_\rho(a):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a),\qquad a\in\Omega.$$

Here $\operatorname{tr}$ is the finite-dimensional endomorphism trace ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

The positivity and normalization of these weights are proved in [[thm-qc-povm-probabilities-normalize]]. A POVM specifies this outcome law; it does not by itself prescribe a conditional output state.

Let $\mathcal H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let
$X:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H$ be self-adjoint. There are non-negative
endomorphisms $X_+,X_-$ such that

$$X=X_+-X_-,\qquad \langle X_+u,X_-v\rangle=0\quad(u,v\in\mathcal H),$$

and

$$\|X\|_1=\operatorname{tr}(X_+)+\operatorname{tr}(X_-).$$

If $\operatorname{tr}(X)=0$, then
$\|X\|_1=2\operatorname{tr}(X_+)=2\operatorname{tr}(X_-)$. 

The trace norm is the finite singular-value norm from
[[def-qc-trace-norm]].

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.

derivations.claim: Let $\Delta=\rho-\sigma=\Delta_+-\Delta_-$. Since $\operatorname{tr}\Delta=0$, [L1] gives $\operatorname{tr}\Delta_+=\operatorname{tr}\Delta_-=D\ge0$, proving the lower bound.

If $\operatorname{supp}\rho\perp\operatorname{supp}\sigma$, then $\rho\sigma=0$ and $\Delta$ acts as $\rho$ on $\operatorname{supp}\rho$, as $-\sigma$ on $\operatorname{supp}\sigma$, and as zero on the orthogonal complement. Hence $\|\Delta\|_1=\operatorname{tr}\rho+\operatorname{tr}\sigma=2$ and $D=1$.

Let $P_+$ project onto the strictly positive eigenspaces of $\Delta$. Then $0\le P_+\le I$ and $D=\operatorname{tr}(P_+\Delta)=\operatorname{tr}(P_+\rho)-\operatorname{tr}(P_+\sigma)\le\operatorname{tr}(P_+\rho)\le1$. The first inequality uses $\operatorname{tr}(P_+\sigma)\ge0$ by [L2], and the last follows from $\operatorname{tr}((I-P_+)\rho)\ge0$ by [L2] and $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$.
If $D=0$, [F1] gives $\|\rho-\sigma\|_1=0$, so definiteness of the trace norm gives $\rho=\sigma$. Conversely equal states have distance zero by [F1].

Conversely, if $D=1$, then both inequalities in step 2.1 are equalities: $\operatorname{tr}(P_+\rho)=1$ and $\operatorname{tr}(P_+\sigma)=0$. Thus $\operatorname{tr}((I-P_+)\rho)=0$ and $\operatorname{tr}(P_+\sigma)=0$. Applying [F3] to each positive operator gives $(I-P_+)\sqrt\rho=0$ and $P_+\sqrt\sigma=0$, so $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq\operatorname{ran}P_+$ and $\operatorname{supp}\sigma\subseteq\ker P_+$. These subspaces are orthogonal.

For every positive integer $d$, the unitary group
$$U(d):=\{U\in M_d(\mathbb C):U^*U=I_d\}$$
is a compact Hausdorff topological group in the Euclidean topology inherited from the real and imaginary parts of its matrix entries.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space, let $k\ge1$, and let $H^{\otimes k}$ use the ordered tensor product register and factor permutation convention of [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]]. For $\pi\in S_k$, let $U_\pi$ be the resulting unitary that permutes the $k$ tensor factors according to $\pi$. Define
$$\Pi_{\mathrm{sym},k}:=\frac1{k!}\sum_{\pi\in S_k}U_\pi.$$
The **symmetric subspace** is $\operatorname{Sym}^k(H):=\{v\in H^{\otimes k}:U_\tau v=v\text{ for every }\tau\in S_k\}$. For $k=0$, the tensor unit is one-dimensional and $\Pi_{\mathrm{sym},0}:=I$.

The permutation average is the orthogonal projector onto $\operatorname{Sym}^k(H)$ by [[lem-qc-symmetric-subspace-average-is-projector]].

Let $H$ be finite-dimensional and let $k\ge1$. The average $\Pi_{\mathrm{sym},k}=\frac1{k!}\sum_{\pi\in S_k}U_\pi$ is self-adjoint and idempotent, with range exactly $\operatorname{Sym}^k(H)=\{v:U_\tau v=v\ \forall\tau\in S_k\}$. For $k=0$ on the tensor unit, $\Pi_{\mathrm{sym},0}=I$ and its range is the full tensor unit.

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Let $(T_k:H_k\to K_k)_{k<n}$ and $(S_k:K_k\to L_k)_{k<n}$ be finite ordered
families of linear maps between finite-dimensional complex inner-product
spaces. Then

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}S_k\right)\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)=\bigotimes_{k<n}(S_kT_k),\qquad \bigotimes_{k<n}I_{H_k}=I_{\otimes_{k<n}H_k},\qquad \left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)^*=\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k^*.$$

In the first formula, $S_kT_k$ means $S_k\circ T_k$. Here $I_{H_k}$ denotes
the identity map $x\mapsto x$. All adjoints use the
repository pairing, linear in the first argument. The empty tensor-map
identity is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on $\mathbb C$.

The sets $\Omega_\alpha$ partition the elementary tensor basis, so the $v_\alpha$ are orthonormal. A vector fixed by all permutations has equal coefficients on each permutation orbit $\Omega_\alpha$; hence these vectors span exactly the symmetric subspace in [F2].

These eigenvalues are distinct: for $\alpha\ne\beta$, let $\ell$ be the first index with $c_\ell:=\alpha_\ell-\beta_\ell\ne0$. Then $|c_\ell|t^\ell\ge t^\ell$, while $|\sum_{j>\ell}c_jt^j|\le k t^{\ell+1}/(1-t)=t^\ell/2$; thus the phase difference is nonzero. Also $|\sum_jc_jt^j|\le kt/(1-t)=1/2<2\pi$, so the phase difference is not a nonzero multiple of $2\pi$.

2.1 Let $W
e\{0\}$ be a subspace invariant under every $U^{\otimes k}$, and choose $0
e w=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha v_\alpha\in W$. At least one coefficient $c_\alpha$ is nonzero. Because the eigenvalues in step 1.2 are distinct, the interpolation polynomial $p_\alpha(z)=\prod_{ eta
e\alpha}(z-\lambda_ eta)/(\lambda_\alpha-\lambda_ eta)$ satisfies $p_\alpha(D^{\otimes k})w=c_\alpha v_\alpha$. Invariance under $D^{\otimes k}$ and linearity imply $v_\alpha\in W$. If $d=1$, step 1.1 has only the single multi-index $(k)$, so this already gives $W=\operatorname{Sym}^k(\mathbb C)$. Hence assume $d\ge2$ in the transfer argument below.

Fix indices $i\ne j$ with $\alpha_i>0$, let $q>0$ be sufficiently small, and set $c=(1+q^2)^{-1/2}$ and $s=q(1+q^2)^{-1/2}$, so $c^2+s^2=1$. Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $\rho,\sigma$ be density operators on $H$ (nonnegative operators of trace one; [[def-qc-density-operator]]). Their **root fidelity** is
$$F(\rho,\sigma):=\|\sqrt\rho\,\sqrt\sigma\|_1,$$
where $\sqrt\rho$ and $\sqrt\sigma$ are the unique non-negative square roots and $\|\cdot\|_1$ is the finite-dimensional trace norm ([[def-qc-trace-norm]]). This library uses root fidelity; the squared quantity $F(\rho,\sigma)^2$ is called squared fidelity.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

Let $A:H\to K$ be a linear map ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional complex
inner-product spaces. Then

$$\|A\|_1=\max\{\,|\operatorname{tr}_H(B^*A)|: B:H\to K\text{ linear and }\|B\|\le1\,\}.$$

Consequently, on the vector space of linear maps $H\to K$, the trace norm is
nonnegative, absolutely homogeneous, definite, and satisfies the triangle
inequality.

Let $T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product space. Then there exist a non-negative endomorphism $U$ and a linear
isometry $S:V\to V$ such that

$$T=SU\qquad\text{and}\qquad U=\sqrt{T^*T}.$$

Equivalently, $S$ is an isometry on $(\ker T)^\perp=\operatorname{im}U$. The
factor $S$ is unique if and only if $T$ is invertible.

derivations.claim: Fix orthonormal bases of $H$ and $R$. Write $x=\sum_{i,a}X_{ia}e_i\otimes f_a$. Directly taking the partial trace gives $\operatorname{Tr}_R|x\rangle\langle x|=XX^*$, while $\|x\|=1$ gives $\operatorname{tr}(XX^*)=1$. Thus purifications of $\rho$ are exactly coefficient matrices $X$ with $XX^*=\rho$ and $\|X\|_2=1$, and the analogous statement holds for $\sigma$.

By [L3], write $X=\sqrt\rho\,W$ and $Y=\sqrt\sigma\,V$, where $W,V:R\to H$ and their adjoints are contractions. Put $A=\sqrt\rho\sqrt\sigma$. The coefficient-matrix inner product [L2] and cyclicity give $|\langle x,y\rangle|=|\operatorname{tr}(XY^*)|=|\operatorname{tr}(\sqrt\sigma\sqrt\rho\,WV^*)|=|\operatorname{tr}(A^*WV^*)|$. Since $WV^*$ is a contraction, [L4] implies $|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|A\|_1=F(\rho,\sigma)$.

Fix the auxiliary space $R$ from the Statement. Since $\dim R\ge\dim H$, choose an isometric embedding $J:H\to R$ using orthonormal bases. Put $A=\sqrt\rho\sqrt\sigma$. By SVD, $\|A^*\|_1=\|A\|_1$, and [L4] supplies a unitary $C$ on $H$ with $|\operatorname{tr}(A^*C)|=\|A\|_1$. Set $X=\sqrt\rho\,J^*$ and $Y=\sqrt\sigma\,C^*J^*$. Then $XX^*=\rho$ and $YY^*=\sigma$, so these coefficient matrices define unit purifications on this fixed $R$. Their overlap satisfies $|\langle x,y\rangle|=|\operatorname{tr}(XY^*)|=|\operatorname{tr}(\sqrt\rho C\sqrt\sigma)|=|\operatorname{tr}(A^*C)|=F(\rho,\sigma)$ by cyclicity. The upper bound in step 1.2 and this attaining pair prove the maximum for every fixed $R$ with $\dim R\ge\dim H$.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space, let $k\ge1$, and let $H^{\otimes k}$ use the ordered tensor product register and factor permutation convention of [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]]. For $\pi\in S_k$, let $U_\pi$ be the resulting unitary that permutes the $k$ tensor factors according to $\pi$. Define
$$\Pi_{\mathrm{sym},k}:=\frac1{k!}\sum_{\pi\in S_k}U_\pi.$$
The **symmetric subspace** is $\operatorname{Sym}^k(H):=\{v\in H^{\otimes k}:U_\tau v=v\text{ for every }\tau\in S_k\}$. For $k=0$, the tensor unit is one-dimensional and $\Pi_{\mathrm{sym},0}:=I$.

The permutation average is the orthogonal projector onto $\operatorname{Sym}^k(H)$ by [[lem-qc-symmetric-subspace-average-is-projector]].

Let $H$ be finite-dimensional and let $k\ge1$. The average $\Pi_{\mathrm{sym},k}=\frac1{k!}\sum_{\pi\in S_k}U_\pi$ is self-adjoint and idempotent, with range exactly $\operatorname{Sym}^k(H)=\{v:U_\tau v=v\ \forall\tau\in S_k\}$. For $k=0$ on the tensor unit, $\Pi_{\mathrm{sym},0}=I$ and its range is the full tensor unit.
For every positive integer $d$ and integer $k\ge0$, the natural unitary action of $U(d)$ on $\operatorname{Sym}^k(\mathbb C^d)$ is irreducible.

For every positive integer $d$, the unitary group
$$U(d):=\{U\in M_d(\mathbb C):U^*U=I_d\}$$
is a compact Hausdorff topological group in the Euclidean topology inherited from the real and imaginary parts of its matrix entries.
Assume AC. Every compact Hausdorff group has a unique left Haar probability measure. It is right invariant and inversion invariant as well.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

$T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism. The endomorphism $T$ is **self-adjoint** when

$$T^*=T,$$

and **normal** when

$$TT^*=T^*T,$$

where $T^*$ is the adjoint from
[[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]].

Every self-adjoint endomorphism is normal, because $TT^*=T^2=T^*T$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

For nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product $H$, the map sending a ray $[u]$ to the rank-one projector $P_u=|u\rangle\langle u|$ of any unit representative is well-defined and bijective onto the rank-one orthogonal projections on $H$. Each $P_u$ is non-negative and has trace one.

derivations.claim: For each weak composition $\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_d=k$ with $\alpha_j\ge0$, sum and normalize the elementary tensors in which index $j$ occurs $\alpha_j$ times. Different compositions have disjoint orthonormal tensor supports, and permutation invariance forces coefficients to be constant on each such orbit, so these vectors form a basis of $\operatorname{Sym}^k(\mathbb C^d)$ by [F1]. Weak compositions correspond bijectively to placements of $d-1$ separators among $k+d-1$ positions (the numbers of stars before, between, and after separators recover the parts). There are $\binom{k+d-1}{d-1}=N_k$ such placements. For $k=0$ this gives the single empty tensor.

The pushforward measure $\mu$ is invariant under every $V\in U(d)$: left invariance of Haar gives $VU$ the same distribution as $U$, and $(VU)e_1=V(Ue_1)$. Define the finite-dimensional operator integral $M=\int |u\rangle\langle u|^{\otimes k}\,d\mu(u)$. By [F5], every integrand is a rank-one projection onto a symmetric tensor and has trace one, so $M=\Pi_{\rm sym}M\Pi_{\rm sym}$ by [F1]. Invariance gives $V^{\otimes k}M(V^{\otimes k})^*=M$.

The coordinate integral in step 1.2 is self-adjoint and nonnegative: each integrand is a rank-one orthogonal projection by [F5], so $M^*=M$ and $\langle Mv,v\rangle=\int|\langle v,u^{\otimes k}\rangle|^2\,d\mu(u)\ge0$. Since $M=\Pi_{\rm sym}M\Pi_{\rm sym}$, its restriction to the symmetric subspace is self-adjoint and nonnegative. By the spectral theorem [F4], that restriction has an orthogonal decomposition into eigenspaces. Each eigenspace is invariant under $U(d)$ because $M$ commutes with the representation by step 1.2; irreducibility [F2] therefore permits only one eigenspace, so $M=c\Pi_{\rm sym}$ for some $c\ge0$. Taking traces gives $1=\operatorname{tr}M=c\operatorname{tr}\Pi_{\rm sym}=cN_k$, since every integrand has trace one by [F5] (also for $k=0$). Thus $c=1/N_k$, proving the moment identity.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $\rho,\sigma$ be density operators on $H$ (nonnegative operators of trace one; [[def-qc-density-operator]]). Their **trace distance** is
$$D(\rho,\sigma):=\tfrac12\|\rho-\sigma\|_1,$$
where $\|\cdot\|_1$ is the trace norm ([[def-qc-trace-norm]]). The factor $1/2$ is part of this state-distance convention. The diamond norm below is an unhalved norm on maps.

Let $\rho,\sigma$ be density operators on a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space and let $\{E_a\}_{a\in\mathcal A}$ be any finite POVM. If $p_a=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a)$ and $q_a=\operatorname{tr}(\sigma E_a)$, then
$$\frac12\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}|p_a-q_a|\le D(\rho,\sigma).$$
The two-effect projective measurement from the Holevo–Helstrom theorem attains equality.

Let $\rho,\sigma$ be density operators on a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space. If they are presented with equal prior probability, the greatest success probability of any binary measurement for identifying the state is
$$\frac12(1+D(\rho,\sigma)).$$
The binary projective measurement whose first effect is the spectral projection of $\Delta=\rho-\sigma$ onto its strictly positive eigenspaces attains this value.

Let $H$ and $K$ be finite-dimensional (have finite bases by [[def-dimension]])
complex inner-product spaces. A
**quantum channel** from $H$ to $K$ is a complex-linear map
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ ([[def-linear-map]]) that is completely
positive ([[def-qc-completely-positive-map]]) and trace-preserving, meaning

$$\operatorname{tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{tr}(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H),$$

where trace is the basis-independent trace of a finite-dimensional
endomorphism ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]). Trace preservation is
required on the full operator space, not only on density operators. This
definition is mathematical and assumes no physical realization.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces, fix an ordered
orthonormal basis $\mathcal B$ of $H$, and let
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ be complex-linear. The following are
equivalent: $\Phi$ is completely positive; $J_{\mathcal B}(\Phi)$ is
non-negative; and $\Phi$ has a finite Kraus representation.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and let
$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a\in A}K_aXK_a^\dagger$ be a finite Kraus representation,
where each $K_a:H\to K$. The map $\Phi$ is trace-preserving on all of
$\mathcal L(H)$, meaning $\operatorname{tr}_K(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{tr}_H(X)$
for every $X\in\mathcal L(H)$, if and only if
$$\sum_{a\in A}K_a^\dagger K_a=I_H.$$

derivations.claim: Let $\{E_a\}_{a\in\mathcal A}$ be any finite POVM on $K$ and choose Kraus operators from [L2]. Define $F_a=\sum_jK_j^*E_aK_j$. For every $x\in H$, $\langle F_ax,x\rangle=\sum_j\langle E_aK_jx,K_jx\rangle\ge0$, so $F_a$ is nonnegative. Completeness follows from $\sum_aF_a=\sum_jK_j^*(\sum_aE_a)K_j=\sum_jK_j^*K_j=I_H$ by [L2]. Thus $\{F_a\}$ is a finite POVM on $H$.

For each outcome, trace cyclicity and the Kraus formula give $\operatorname{tr}(\Phi(\rho)E_a)=\sum_j\operatorname{tr}(K_j\rho K_j^*E_a)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_a)$, and likewise for $\sigma$. Their output total variation is therefore the total variation of the pulled-back POVM and is at most $D(\rho,\sigma)$ by [L1]. Maximizing over output POVMs gives $D(\Phi(\rho),\Phi(\sigma))$ by the Helstrom formula in [L1], proving contractivity, including $\rho=\sigma$.
