citations.quote:
Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $\rho,\sigma\in\mathcal D(H)$. For every auxiliary space $R$ with $\dim R\ge\dim H$, a **purification** of $\rho$ on $H\otimes R$ means a unit vector $x$ with $\operatorname{Tr}_R(|x\rangle\langle x|)=\rho$. Then
$$F(\rho,\sigma)=\max\{|\langle x,y\rangle|:x,y\in H\otimes R,\ \|x\|=\|y\|=1,\ \operatorname{Tr}_R|x\rangle\langle x|=\rho,\ \operatorname{Tr}_R|y\rangle\langle y|=\sigma\}.$$
In particular, the maximum is attained with $R\cong H$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space; the pairing is linear in its first argument ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for its complex-linear endomorphisms ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]) and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite POVM** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $E=(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ with each $E_a$ nonnegative and $\sum_{a\in\Omega}E_a=I_H$; after any enumeration of $\Omega$, these operators form the finite complete positive family of [[def-qc-finite-positive-effect-family]]. Reordering does not alter the finite sum. The complete-family lemma [[lem-qc-complete-effect-family-members-are-effects]] shows that every $E_a$ also has nonnegative complement $I_H-E_a$, so each is an effect.

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (a nonnegative operator of trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), its **POVM outcome weights** are

$$p_\rho(a):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a),\qquad a\in\Omega.$$

Here $\operatorname{tr}$ is the finite-dimensional endomorphism trace ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

The positivity and normalization of these weights are proved in [[thm-qc-povm-probabilities-normalize]]. A POVM specifies this outcome law; it does not by itself prescribe a conditional output state.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

For density operators $\rho,\sigma$ on a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space,
$$\|\sqrt\rho\,\sqrt\sigma\|_1=\operatorname{tr}\sqrt{\sqrt\rho\,\sigma\,\sqrt\rho}.$$

For every positive integer $d$, the unitary group
$$U(d):=\{U\in M_d(\mathbb C):U^*U=I_d\}$$
is a compact Hausdorff topological group in the Euclidean topology inherited from the real and imaginary parts of its matrix entries.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

Let $A:H\to K$ be a linear map ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional complex
inner-product spaces. Then

$$\|A\|_1=\max\{\,|\operatorname{tr}_H(B^*A)|: B:H\to K\text{ linear and }\|B\|\le1\,\}.$$

Consequently, on the vector space of linear maps $H\to K$, the trace norm is
nonnegative, absolutely homogeneous, definite, and satisfies the triangle
inequality.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $A:H\to K$ be a linear map ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces. Its singular values are the eigenvalues of
$|A|:=\sqrt{A^*A}:H\to H$, counted with multiplicity, as defined in
[[def-singular-values-of-an-endomorphism]]. Define the **trace norm**, or
Schatten-$1$ norm, by

$$\|A\|_1:=\sum_{j<\dim H}s_j(A).$$

The sum includes zero singular values and is $0$ when $H$ is the zero space.
For this definition, $A$ may be rectangular; the singular values are those of
$|A|$ on the domain $H$. The spectral trace formula is proved in
[[thm-qc-trace-norm-spectral-formula]].
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.

derivations.claim: Let $x,y$ be purifications attaining $F(\rho,\sigma)$ as in [L1]. For a finite POVM $(E_a)$, put $x_a=(\sqrt{E_a}\otimes I)x$ and $y_a=(\sqrt{E_a}\otimes I)y$. Since $\sum_a E_a=I$, the adjoint identity gives $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_a\langle x_a,y_a\rangle$. By [L4], $\|x_a\|^2=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a)$ and $\|y_a\|^2=\operatorname{tr}(\sigma E_a)$. The triangle inequality and [F1] termwise give $|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\sum_a\|x_a\|\|y_a\|=\sum_a\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a)\operatorname{tr}(\sigma E_a)}$. Therefore every finite POVM overlap is at least $F(\rho,\sigma)$.

For arbitrary $\rho,\sigma$, set $\rho_\varepsilon=(1-\varepsilon)\rho+\varepsilon I/d$ and $\sigma_\varepsilon=(1-\varepsilon)\sigma+\varepsilon I/d$ for $0<\varepsilon\le1$. Both are positive definite. The root fidelity is continuous on density operators: if $A_n\to A$ are density operators and $B_n=\sqrt{A_n}$, then [F5] and [F7] give $\sum_{i,j}|(B_n)_{ij}|^2=\operatorname{tr}(B_n^*B_n)=1$. Thus the coordinate matrices $B_n$ are bounded. Every convergent subsequence has a nonnegative limit $B$ by [F6] and $B^2=A$, so uniqueness in [L3] gives $B=\sqrt A$. If $(B_n)$ did not converge to $\sqrt A$, a subsequence staying a fixed positive distance away would have a convergent subsubsequence by [F2], contradicting that every such limit is $\sqrt A$. Applying this to both state sequences shows their square roots converge; their product converges by the finite matrix-product formula, and its trace norm converges by [L5]. Hence $F(\rho_\varepsilon,\sigma_\varepsilon)\to F(\rho,\sigma)$.

Suppose first that $\rho$ is positive definite. By [F4], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis of $\rho$; its eigenvalues are strictly positive by positive definiteness, so $\rho^{-1/2}$ is defined by the reciprocal square roots in this basis. Define $M=\rho^{-1/2}(\sqrt\rho\,\sigma\sqrt\rho)^{1/2}\rho^{-1/2}$. Its quadratic form is nonnegative because it is the quadratic form of $(\sqrt\rho\,\sigma\sqrt\rho)^{1/2}$ at $\rho^{-1/2}x$, and direct multiplication gives $M\rho M=\sigma$. By [F4], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis of $M$, with rank-one projections $E_j$ and eigenvalues $\mu_j\ge0$. If $p_j=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_j)$, then $\operatorname{tr}(\sigma E_j)=\mu_j^2p_j$, so the measurement overlap is $\sum_j\mu_jp_j=\operatorname{tr}(M\rho)=\operatorname{tr}(\sqrt{\sqrt\rho\,\sigma\sqrt\rho})=F(\rho,\sigma)$ by [L3] and [L6]. Thus a rank-one PVM attains the lower bound when $\rho$ is faithful.

Fix an orthonormal basis of $H$ by [F3], and identify $H$ with $\mathbb C^d$. Let $Q_j$ be the rank-one projector onto its $j$th basis vector. Define $\mathcal P_d$ as ordered families $(UQ_jU^*)_{j=1}^d$ for $U\in U(d)$. Every ordered rank-one PVM has this form, since unit vectors spanning its mutually orthogonal one-dimensional ranges form an orthonormal basis. The map $U\mapsto(UQ_jU^*)_{j=1}^d$ is continuous in matrix coordinates, so $\mathcal P_d$ is compact by [F2]. For every $\varepsilon>0$, step 2.1 supplies a minimizing PVM in $\mathcal P_d$. For $n\ge1$, let $C_n$ be the closure in $\mathcal P_d$ of all such minimizing PVMs for $0<\varepsilon<1/n$. The $C_n$ are nonempty nested compact sets, so their intersection is nonempty; fix $P_0$ in it. The overlap function $g(\varepsilon,P)=\sum_j\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\varepsilon P_j)\operatorname{tr}(\sigma_\varepsilon P_j)}$ is continuous at every $(0,P_0)$, since trace is a finite coordinate sum and scalar square root is continuous on $[0,\infty)$. Given $\delta>0$, choose a neighborhood of $(0,P_0)$ where $g$ differs from $g(0,P_0)$ by less than $\delta$, and choose $n$ so large that $1/n$ is inside its $\varepsilon$-neighborhood and, by step 1.2, $|F(\rho_\varepsilon,\sigma_\varepsilon)-F(\rho,\sigma)|<\delta$ for $0<\varepsilon<1/n$. Since $P_0\in C_n$, the definition of closure supplies a minimizing PVM $P'$ in that neighborhood for some $0<\varepsilon<1/n$. For this pair, $g(\varepsilon,P')=F(\rho_\varepsilon,\sigma_\varepsilon)$, so $|g(0,P_0)-F(\rho,\sigma)|<2\delta$. As $\delta>0$ is arbitrary, $g(0,P_0)=F(\rho,\sigma)$. This gives an attaining rank-one PVM also in the singular case.
Step 1.1 bounds every finite POVM overlap below by $F$, and step 3.1 exhibits a finite rank-one PVM whose overlap equals $F$. This proves the stated minimum and attainment.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space, let $k\ge1$, and let $H^{\otimes k}$ use the ordered tensor product register and factor permutation convention of [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]]. For $\pi\in S_k$, let $U_\pi$ be the resulting unitary that permutes the $k$ tensor factors according to $\pi$. Define
$$\Pi_{\mathrm{sym},k}:=\frac1{k!}\sum_{\pi\in S_k}U_\pi.$$
The **symmetric subspace** is $\operatorname{Sym}^k(H):=\{v\in H^{\otimes k}:U_\tau v=v\text{ for every }\tau\in S_k\}$. For $k=0$, the tensor unit is one-dimensional and $\Pi_{\mathrm{sym},0}:=I$.

The permutation average is the orthogonal projector onto $\operatorname{Sym}^k(H)$ by [[lem-qc-symmetric-subspace-average-is-projector]].

Let $H$ be finite-dimensional and let $k\ge1$. The average $\Pi_{\mathrm{sym},k}=\frac1{k!}\sum_{\pi\in S_k}U_\pi$ is self-adjoint and idempotent, with range exactly $\operatorname{Sym}^k(H)=\{v:U_\tau v=v\ \forall\tau\in S_k\}$. For $k=0$ on the tensor unit, $\Pi_{\mathrm{sym},0}=I$ and its range is the full tensor unit.

Assume the axiom-of-choice branch used by [[cor-normalized-haar-probability-on-a-compact-group]]. For integers $d\ge1$ and $k\ge0$, put $N_k=\binom{k+d-1}{d-1}$. Then $\dim\operatorname{Sym}^k(\mathbb C^d)=N_k$, and if $\mu$ is the probability measure on the unit sphere obtained by pushing normalized Haar probability on $U(d)$ through $U\mapsto Ue_1$, then
$$\int |u\rangle\langle u|^{\otimes k}\,d\mu(u)=\frac{1}{N_k}\Pi_{\mathrm{sym},k}.$$
For $k=0$, the tensor power and projector are the identity on the one-dimensional tensor unit.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and let
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ have a finite Kraus representation
$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a\in A}K_a X K_a^\dagger$. Then $\Phi$ is completely positive.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.

Let $H$ and $K$ be finite-dimensional (have finite bases by [[def-dimension]])
complex inner-product spaces. A
**quantum channel** from $H$ to $K$ is a complex-linear map
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ ([[def-linear-map]]) that is completely
positive ([[def-qc-completely-positive-map]]) and trace-preserving, meaning

$$\operatorname{tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{tr}(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H),$$

where trace is the basis-independent trace of a finite-dimensional
endomorphism ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]). Trace preservation is
required on the full operator space, not only on density operators. This
definition is mathematical and assumes no physical realization.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

derivations.claim: Put $E=I-\Pi_{\rm sym,n}\ge0$ by [L1], so $E^{1/2}$ exists by [F5]. The first summand of $\Phi$ is completely positive: by [F4], choose an orthonormal product basis $(g_j)$ of the added registers and set $A_j=\sqrt{N_n/N_m}\,\Pi_{\rm sym,m}(I\otimes|g_j\rangle)$. Then $\sum_jA_jXA_j^*=\frac{N_n}{N_m}\Pi_{\rm sym,m}(X\otimes I^{\otimes(m-n)})\Pi_{\rm sym,m}$. When $m=n$, the added tensor unit has its single basis vector and this map is the identity before compression. By [F3], write $\omega=\sum_\ell s_\ell|f_\ell\rangle\langle f_\ell|$ in an orthonormal eigenbasis and choose an input orthonormal basis $(e_j)$ by [F4]. The second summand has Kraus operators $K_{\ell j}=\sqrt{s_\ell}|f_\ell\rangle\langle e_j|E^{1/2}$, using [F6] and the outer-product convention, since $\sum_{\ell,j}K_{\ell j}XK_{\ell j}^*=\operatorname{tr}(EX)\omega$. Thus both summands and their sum are completely positive by the finite Kraus theorem [L3].

The Haar moment [L2], followed by the coordinate partial trace over the last $m-n$ factors, gives $\operatorname{Tr}_{m-n}(\Pi_{\rm sym,m})=(N_m/N_n)\Pi_{\rm sym,n}$, because each product-basis partial trace sends $|u\rangle\langle u|^{\otimes m}$ to $|u\rangle\langle u|^{\otimes n}$. Finite-dimensionality allows the partial trace to pass through the coordinatewise integral. Therefore $$\operatorname{tr}\!\left(\frac{N_n}{N_m}\Pi_{\rm sym,m}(X\otimes I)\Pi_{\rm sym,m}\right)=\operatorname{tr}(X\Pi_{\rm sym,n}),$$ where cyclicity, $\Pi_{\rm sym,m}^2=\Pi_{\rm sym,m}$, and [L3] were used. The second summand has trace $\operatorname{tr}(EX)\operatorname{tr}(\omega)=\operatorname{tr}(EX)$ by [F2]. Their sum is $\operatorname{tr}X$, so [F1] and step 1.1 make $\Phi$ a channel.

For unit $u$, $|u\rangle^{\otimes n}$ lies in the symmetric subspace, so the second summand vanishes. Also $|u\rangle^{\otimes m}$ is fixed by $\Pi_{\rm sym,m}$. Its expectation in the first summand is therefore $(N_n/N_m)\langle u^{\otimes m}|(|u\rangle\langle u|^{\otimes n}\otimes I)|u^{\otimes m}\rangle=N_n/N_m$. This value is independent of $u$, proving the claim.

derivations.claim: Choose a finite Kraus family $(A_a)$ from [L3], and write $\Pi_n=\Pi_{\rm sym,n}$ and $\Pi_m=\Pi_{\rm sym,m}$. For each unit $u$, put $v=u^{\otimes n}$, $w=u^{\otimes m}$, and $f(u)=\operatorname{tr}(\Phi(|v\rangle\langle v|)|w\rangle\langle w|)$. By [L2], this is the squared root fidelity in the Statement. Since $v$ is a unit symmetric tensor, $\Pi_n v=v$ by [F1]. The Kraus formula, the rank-one convention, and Cauchy–Schwarz [F3] give $f(u)=\sum_a|\langle A_av,w\rangle|^2=\sum_a|\langle v,\Pi_n A_a^*w\rangle|^2\le\sum_a\|\Pi_n A_a^*w\|^2=\langle Cw,w\rangle$, where $C=\sum_aA_a\Pi_n A_a^*$ is self-adjoint and nonnegative: each quadratic form is $\|\Pi_n A_a^*w\|^2$.

Integrating this pointwise bound and applying the $m$-th Haar moment [L1] yields $\int f(u)d\mu(u)\le\operatorname{tr}(C\Pi_m)/N_m$. Since $C$ and $I-\Pi_m$ are nonnegative by step 1.1 and [F1], [F2] gives $\operatorname{tr}(C(I-\Pi_m))\ge0$, hence $\operatorname{tr}(C\Pi_m)\le\operatorname{tr}C$. Trace cyclicity [F2], normalization [L3], and [L1] give $\operatorname{tr}C=\sum_a\operatorname{tr}(\Pi_nA_a^*A_a)=\operatorname{tr}\Pi_n=N_n$. Therefore $\int f(u)d\mu(u)\le N_n/N_m$. The function $f$ is continuous in the finite coordinates of $u$, hence measurable; because $\mu$ is a probability measure, its infimum is no larger than its average. Thus $\inf_{\|u\|=1}f(u)\le N_n/N_m$, including $d=1$ and $n=m$.

Let $H,K$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces and let $\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ be complex-linear. For each finite $r\ge1$, the induced trace norm of the amplification is
$$\|\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb C^r}\|_{1\to1}:=\sup_{X\ne0}\frac{\| (\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb C^r})(X)\|_1}{\|X\|_1},$$
where $X\in\mathcal L(H\otimes\mathbb C^r)$ and $\|\cdot\|_1$ is the finite-dimensional trace norm ([[def-qc-trace-norm]]). The **diamond norm** (the completely bounded trace norm) is
$$\|\Phi\|_\diamond:=\sup_{r\ge1}\|\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb C^r}\|_{1\to1}.$$
There is no factor $1/2$ in this map norm. The finite-dimensional ancilla theorem [[thm-qc-diamond-norm-ancilla-dimension-bound]] proves the supremum is finite, is attained, and can be capped at $r=\dim H$.

Let $H,K$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces, $d=\dim H$, and let $\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ be linear. Then
$$\|\Phi\|_\diamond=\|\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb C^d}\|_{1\to1},$$
and the latter induced norm is attained on some rank-one operator $R_{x,y}:z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{\rm root}x$ with unit vectors $x,y\in H\otimes\mathbb C^d$.

Let $H$ and $K$ be finite-dimensional (have finite bases by [[def-dimension]])
complex inner-product spaces. A
**quantum channel** from $H$ to $K$ is a complex-linear map
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ ([[def-linear-map]]) that is completely
positive ([[def-qc-completely-positive-map]]) and trace-preserving, meaning

$$\operatorname{tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{tr}(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H),$$

where trace is the basis-independent trace of a finite-dimensional
endomorphism ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]). Trace preservation is
required on the full operator space, not only on density operators. This
definition is mathematical and assumes no physical realization.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces, fix an ordered
orthonormal basis $\mathcal B$ of $H$, and let
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ be complex-linear. The following are
equivalent: $\Phi$ is completely positive; $J_{\mathcal B}(\Phi)$ is
non-negative; and $\Phi$ has a finite Kraus representation.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and let
$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a\in A}K_aXK_a^\dagger$ be a finite Kraus representation,
where each $K_a:H\to K$. The map $\Phi$ is trace-preserving on all of
$\mathcal L(H)$, meaning $\operatorname{tr}_K(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{tr}_H(X)$
for every $X\in\mathcal L(H)$, if and only if
$$\sum_{a\in A}K_a^\dagger K_a=I_H.$$

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and let
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ have a finite Kraus representation
$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a\in A}K_a X K_a^\dagger$. Then $\Phi$ is completely positive.

Let $A:H\to K$ be a linear map ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional complex
inner-product spaces. Then

$$\|A\|_1=\max\{\,|\operatorname{tr}_H(B^*A)|: B:H\to K\text{ linear and }\|B\|\le1\,\}.$$

Consequently, on the vector space of linear maps $H\to K$, the trace norm is
nonnegative, absolutely homogeneous, definite, and satisfies the triangle
inequality.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

Let $(T_k:H_k\to K_k)_{k<n}$ and $(S_k:K_k\to L_k)_{k<n}$ be finite ordered
families of linear maps between finite-dimensional complex inner-product
spaces. Then

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}S_k\right)\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)=\bigotimes_{k<n}(S_kT_k),\qquad \bigotimes_{k<n}I_{H_k}=I_{\otimes_{k<n}H_k},\qquad \left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)^*=\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k^*.$$

In the first formula, $S_kT_k$ means $S_k\circ T_k$. Here $I_{H_k}$ denotes
the identity map $x\mapsto x$. All adjoints use the
repository pairing, linear in the first argument. The empty tensor-map
identity is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on $\mathbb C$.

Let $H,H'$ be finite-dimensional (have finite bases by [[def-dimension]])
complex inner-product spaces with ordered
orthonormal bases $(e_u)_{u<n}$ and $(f_s)_{s<m}$. For $u,v<n$ and $s,t<m$
define $E_{uv}x:=\langle x,e_v\rangle e_u$ and
$F_{st}y:=\langle y,f_t\rangle f_s$. Then
$(E_{uv}\otimes F_{st})_{u,v,s,t}$ is a basis of
$\mathcal L(H\otimes H')$. Empty dimensions give the empty basis of the zero
endomorphism space. The root pairing is linear in its first argument, so the
displayed matrix-unit maps are linear.

Let $A:H\to K$ be a linear map ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces. Its singular values are the eigenvalues of
$|A|:=\sqrt{A^*A}:H\to H$, counted with multiplicity, as defined in
[[def-singular-values-of-an-endomorphism]]. Define the **trace norm**, or
Schatten-$1$ norm, by

$$\|A\|_1:=\sum_{j<\dim H}s_j(A).$$

The sum includes zero singular values and is $0$ when $H$ is the zero space.
For this definition, $A$ may be rectangular; the singular values are those of
$|A|$ on the domain $H$. The spectral trace formula is proved in
[[thm-qc-trace-norm-spectral-formula]].

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

For nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product $H$, the map sending a ray $[u]$ to the rank-one projector $P_u=|u\rangle\langle u|$ of any unit representative is well-defined and bijective onto the rank-one orthogonal projections on $H$. Each $P_u$ is non-negative and has trace one.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

derivations.claim: By [L1], it suffices to use the ancilla $R=\mathbb C^d$, where $d=\dim H$. Let $\Lambda=\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_R$. By [L4], its Kraus operators are $K_j\otimes I_R$, and [L6] ensures this factorwise Kraus formula agrees with the amplification on every operator. Its trace-preserving normalization follows from [L2]. Define $\Lambda^*(B)=\sum_j(K_j^*\otimes I_R)B(K_j\otimes I_R)$. It is completely positive by [L3] and unital because $\sum_j(K_j^*\otimes I_R)(K_j\otimes I_R)=I$. If $\|B\|_\infty\le1$, then $\begin{pmatrix}I&B\\B^*&I\end{pmatrix}$ is nonnegative: for any $(x,y)$ its quadratic form is at least $\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2-2\|x\|\|y\|\ge0$ by [F2]–[F3]. Complete positivity of $\Lambda^*$ applied with the two-dimensional auxiliary space preserves this block positivity. For $T=\Lambda^*(B)$, test the resulting block operator on $(-Ty,y)$; its quadratic form is $\|y\|^2-\|Ty\|^2$, so $\|\Lambda^*(B)\|_\infty\le1$.

For any input operator $X$, the Kraus formula for $\Lambda^*$ and cyclicity [F2] give $\operatorname{tr}(B^*\Lambda(X))=\operatorname{tr}(\Lambda^*(B)^*X)$. Trace-norm duality [L3] then gives $$\|\Lambda(X)\|_1=\max_{\|B\|_\infty\le1}|\operatorname{tr}(B^*\Lambda(X))|=\max_{\|B\|_\infty\le1}|\operatorname{tr}(\Lambda^*(B)^*X)|\le\|X\|_1,$$ using step 1.1. Thus the induced norm at ancilla dimension $d$ is at most one, and [L1] gives $\|\Phi\|_\diamond\le1$. Conversely choose unit vectors $x\in H$ and $e\in\mathbb C^d$. The rank-one projector $P=|x\otimes e\rangle\langle x\otimes e|$ is a density operator by [L5]. The amplified map $\Lambda$ is completely positive by [L3] and trace-preserving by [L2] and [L4], so $\Lambda(P)$ is a density operator and has trace norm one by [F1]. Therefore the induced norm at $d$ is at least one, and [L1] gives $\|\Phi\|_\diamond\ge1$.

positive ([[def-qc-completely-positive-map]]) and trace-preserving, meaning

$$\operatorname{tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{tr}(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H),$$

where trace is the basis-independent trace of a finite-dimensional
endomorphism ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]). Trace preservation is
required on the full operator space, not only on density operators. This
definition is mathematical and assumes no physical realization.

Let $H,K$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces and let $\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ be complex-linear. For each finite $r\ge1$, the induced trace norm of the amplification is
$$\|\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb C^r}\|_{1\to1}:=\sup_{X\ne0}\frac{\| (\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb C^r})(X)\|_1}{\|X\|_1},$$
where $X\in\mathcal L(H\otimes\mathbb C^r)$ and $\|\cdot\|_1$ is the finite-dimensional trace norm ([[def-qc-trace-norm]]). The **diamond norm** (the completely bounded trace norm) is
$$\|\Phi\|_\diamond:=\sup_{r\ge1}\|\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb C^r}\|_{1\to1}.$$
There is no factor $1/2$ in this map norm. The finite-dimensional ancilla theorem [[thm-qc-diamond-norm-ancilla-dimension-bound]] proves the supremum is finite, is attained, and can be capped at $r=\dim H$.

Let $H,K$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces, $d=\dim H$, and let $\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ be linear. Then
$$\|\Phi\|_\diamond=\|\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb C^d}\|_{1\to1},$$
and the latter induced norm is attained on some rank-one operator $R_{x,y}:z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{\rm root}x$ with unit vectors $x,y\in H\otimes\mathbb C^d$.

Let $A:H\to K$ be a linear map ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional complex
inner-product spaces. Then

$$\|A\|_1=\max\{\,|\operatorname{tr}_H(B^*A)|: B:H\to K\text{ linear and }\|B\|\le1\,\}.$$

Consequently, on the vector space of linear maps $H\to K$, the trace norm is
nonnegative, absolutely homogeneous, definite, and satisfies the triangle
inequality.
Every quantum channel $\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ between nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces has $\|\Phi\|_\diamond=1$.

$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ be a quantum channel. It has a finite
Kraus representation, and for any chosen such representation with $N$
operators $K_a:H\to K$ there are an $N$-dimensional environment $E$ and a
linear isometry $V:H\to K\otimes E$ such that
$$\Phi(X)=\operatorname{Tr}_E(VXV^\dagger)\quad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H).$$

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $\rho,\sigma\in\mathcal D(H)$. For every auxiliary space $R$ with $\dim R\ge\dim H$, a **purification** of $\rho$ on $H\otimes R$ means a unit vector $x$ with $\operatorname{Tr}_R(|x\rangle\langle x|)=\rho$. Then
$$F(\rho,\sigma)=\max\{|\langle x,y\rangle|:x,y\in H\otimes R,\ \|x\|=\|y\|=1,\ \operatorname{Tr}_R|x\rangle\langle x|=\rho,\ \operatorname{Tr}_R|y\rangle\langle y|=\sigma\}.$$
In particular, the maximum is attained with $R\cong H$.

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $\rho,\sigma$ be density operators on $H$ (nonnegative operators of trace one; [[def-qc-density-operator]]). Their **trace distance** is
$$D(\rho,\sigma):=\tfrac12\|\rho-\sigma\|_1,$$
where $\|\cdot\|_1$ is the trace norm ([[def-qc-trace-norm]]). The factor $1/2$ is part of this state-distance convention. The diamond norm below is an unhalved norm on maps.

$$\frac12\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}|p_a-q_a|\le D(\rho,\sigma).$$

In particular, the maximum is attained with $R\cong H$.

For unit vectors $u,v$ in a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space, let $P_u=|u\rangle\langle u|$ and $P_v=|v\rangle\langle v|$. Then
$$D(P_u,P_v)=\sqrt{1-|\langle u|v\rangle_D|^2},$$
where $\langle\cdot|\cdot\rangle_D$ is the Dirac pairing converted from the root library's first-argument-linear inner product.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Assume the choice branch in [[thm-qc-symmetric-subspace-dimension-and-haar-moment]]. Let $d\ge1$ and $1\le n\le m$. Every channel $\Phi:\mathcal L((\mathbb C^d)^{\otimes n})\to\mathcal L((\mathbb C^d)^{\otimes m})$ has
$$\inf_{\|u\|=1}F\!\left(\Phi(|u\rangle\langle u|^{\otimes n}),|u\rangle\langle u|^{\otimes m}\right)^2\le\frac{N_n}{N_m},\qquad N_r=\binom{r+d-1}{d-1}.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the choice branch in [[thm-qc-symmetric-subspace-dimension-and-haar-moment]]. Let $d\ge1$ and $1\le n\le m$. Write $N_r=\binom{r+d-1}{d-1}$ and let $\Pi_{\rm sym,r}$ project onto $\operatorname{Sym}^r(\mathbb C^d)$. For any fixed output density operator $\omega$ on $(\mathbb C^d)^{\otimes m}$, the map
$$\Phi(X)=\frac{N_n}{N_m}\Pi_{\rm sym,m}(X\otimes I^{\otimes(m-n)})\Pi_{\rm sym,m}+\operatorname{tr}((I-\Pi_{\rm sym,n})X)\,\omega$$
is a channel and satisfies $\operatorname{tr}(\Phi(|u\rangle\langle u|^{\otimes n})|u\rangle\langle u|^{\otimes m})=N_n/N_m$ for every unit $u\in\mathbb C^d$.

citations.quote: Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space. Two nonzero vectors $x,y\in H$ represent the same **ray** when $y=\alpha x$ for some nonzero $\alpha\in\mathbb C$. A **pure state** is such a ray. If $u$ is a unit representative, its associated operator is $P_u=|u\rangle\langle u|$, with the bra, ket and outer-product convention of [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]]. The theorem [[thm-qc-ray-projector-well-defined-and-bijective]] proves that this operator is a rank-one orthogonal projection independent of the chosen unit representative, so it is the operator representative of the pure state.

For nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product $H$, the map sending a ray $[u]$ to the rank-one projector $P_u=|u\rangle\langle u|$ of any unit representative is well-defined and bijective onto the rank-one orthogonal projections on $H$. Each $P_u$ is non-negative and has trace one.

Let $H$ and $K$ be finite-dimensional (have finite bases by [[def-dimension]])
complex inner-product spaces. A
**quantum channel** from $H$ to $K$ is a complex-linear map
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ ([[def-linear-map]]) that is completely
positive ([[def-qc-completely-positive-map]]) and trace-preserving, meaning

$$\operatorname{tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{tr}(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H),$$

where trace is the basis-independent trace of a finite-dimensional
endomorphism ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]). Trace preservation is
required on the full operator space, not only on density operators. This
definition is mathematical and assumes no physical realization.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and let
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ be a quantum channel. It has a finite
Kraus representation, and for any chosen such representation with $N$
operators $K_a:H\to K$ there are an $N$-dimensional environment $E$ and a
linear isometry $V:H\to K\otimes E$ such that
$$\Phi(X)=\operatorname{Tr}_E(VXV^\dagger)\quad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H).$$

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex-inner-product spaces with the tensor-product convention of [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]]. For every $\Psi\in H\otimes K$ there are an integer $r\ge0$, positive numbers $s_1,\ldots,s_r$, and orthonormal families $u_1,\ldots,u_r\in H$ and $v_1,\ldots,v_r\in K$ such that

$$\Psi=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j u_j\otimes v_j,\qquad \|\Psi\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j^2.$$

For $\Psi=0$ take $r=0$ and the empty sum. For any chosen ordered pair of orthonormal bases, the construction below obtains the $s_j$ as the positive singular values of the coefficient matrix of $\Psi$ in their ordered product basis.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

Let $H,K,E$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and let
$V:H\to K\otimes E$ be a linear isometry. Then
$$\Phi(X)=\operatorname{Tr}_E(VXV^\dagger),\qquad X\in\mathcal L(H),$$
is a quantum channel from $H$ to $K$.

derivations.claim: For each unit representative $\psi$ of a ray in $S$, the reduced state of $V\psi$ on the two output registers is the pure projector $P_\psi\otimes P_\psi$. By the Schmidt decomposition [L3], there is a unit environment vector $e_\psi$ and a phase absorbed into it such that $V\psi=\psi\otimes\psi\otimes e_\psi$.

For any two unit representatives $\psi,\phi\in S$, the isometry preserves their inner product. By step 1.1, $$\langle\psi,\phi\rangle=\langle V\psi,V\phi\rangle=\langle\psi,\phi\rangle^2\langle e_\psi,e_\phi\rangle.$$ Taking absolute values and applying Cauchy–Schwarz to the unit environment vectors gives $c=c^2|\langle e_\psi,e_\phi\rangle|\le c^2$, where $c=|\langle\psi,\phi\rangle|\in[0,1]$. Hence $c(1-c)\le0$ with both factors nonnegative, so $c=0$ or $c=1$. The first case is orthogonality; in the second, equality in Cauchy–Schwarz makes the two vectors scalar multiples and their rays identical ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]).

If $\dim H\ge2$, choose orthonormal $e_1,e_2$; the rays of $e_1$ and $(e_1+e_2)/\sqrt2$ are neither equal nor orthogonal, contradicting step 2.1 for a universal exact cloner. If $\dim H=1$, fix a unit vector $e$ and take the one-dimensional environment $E=\mathbb C$ with unit vector $f$. Define $V(e)=e\otimes e\otimes f$ and extend linearly; because this sends the unit basis vector to a unit product vector, it is an isometry. By [L4], $X\mapsto\operatorname{Tr}_E(VXV^*)$ is a channel; on the sole pure-state projector it outputs $P_e\otimes P_e$. Hence the unique ray is cloned by a channel.

Let $H,K$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces and let $\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ be complex-linear. For each finite $r\ge1$, the induced trace norm of the amplification is
$$\|\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb C^r}\|_{1\to1}:=\sup_{X\ne0}\frac{\| (\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb C^r})(X)\|_1}{\|X\|_1},$$
where $X\in\mathcal L(H\otimes\mathbb C^r)$ and $\|\cdot\|_1$ is the finite-dimensional trace norm ([[def-qc-trace-norm]]). The **diamond norm** (the completely bounded trace norm) is
$$\|\Phi\|_\diamond:=\sup_{r\ge1}\|\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb C^r}\|_{1\to1}.$$
There is no factor $1/2$ in this map norm. The finite-dimensional ancilla theorem [[thm-qc-diamond-norm-ancilla-dimension-bound]] proves the supremum is finite, is attained, and can be capped at $r=\dim H$.

Let $H,K$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces, $d=\dim H$, and let $\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ be linear. Then
$$\|\Phi\|_\diamond=\|\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb C^d}\|_{1\to1},$$
and the latter induced norm is attained on some rank-one operator $R_{x,y}:z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{\rm root}x$ with unit vectors $x,y\in H\otimes\mathbb C^d$.

For finite-dimensional complex-inner-product spaces $H_1,K_1,H_2,K_2$ and linear maps $A:H_1\to K_1$, $B:H_2\to K_2$,
$$\|A\otimes B\|_1=\|A\|_1\,\|B\|_1.$$
The equality includes zero maps and zero-dimensional factors.

Let $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$ be a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces, with the product bases of
[[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]]. For a permutation $\sigma$ of the
factor positions, the map $P_\sigma$ that reorders the factors is a bijective
linear isometry from $H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$ to
$H_{\sigma(0)}\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{\sigma(n-1)}$. When source and target
are identified as the same register, $P_\sigma$ is a unitary operator in the
sense of [[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]].

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

Let $(T_k:H_k\to K_k)_{k<n}$ and $(S_k:K_k\to L_k)_{k<n}$ be finite ordered
families of linear maps between finite-dimensional complex inner-product
spaces. Then

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}S_k\right)\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)=\bigotimes_{k<n}(S_kT_k),\qquad \bigotimes_{k<n}I_{H_k}=I_{\otimes_{k<n}H_k},\qquad \left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)^*=\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k^*.$$

In the first formula, $S_kT_k$ means $S_k\circ T_k$. Here $I_{H_k}$ denotes
the identity map $x\mapsto x$. All adjoints use the
repository pairing, linear in the first argument. The empty tensor-map
identity is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on $\mathbb C$.

Let $H,H'$ be finite-dimensional (have finite bases by [[def-dimension]])
complex inner-product spaces with ordered
orthonormal bases $(e_u)_{u<n}$ and $(f_s)_{s<m}$. For $u,v<n$ and $s,t<m$
define $E_{uv}x:=\langle x,e_v\rangle e_u$ and
$F_{st}y:=\langle y,f_t\rangle f_s$. Then
$(E_{uv}\otimes F_{st})_{u,v,s,t}$ is a basis of
$\mathcal L(H\otimes H')$. Empty dimensions give the empty basis of the zero
endomorphism space. The root pairing is linear in its first argument, so the
displayed matrix-unit maps are linear.

Let $A:H\to K$ be a linear map ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional complex
inner-product spaces. Then

$$\|A\|_1=\max\{\,|\operatorname{tr}_H(B^*A)|: B:H\to K\text{ linear and }\|B\|\le1\,\}.$$

Consequently, on the vector space of linear maps $H\to K$, the trace norm is
nonnegative, absolutely homogeneous, definite, and satisfies the triangle
inequality.

Let $H$ and $K$ be finite-dimensional (have finite bases by [[def-dimension]])
complex inner-product spaces. A
**quantum channel** from $H$ to $K$ is a complex-linear map
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ ([[def-linear-map]]) that is completely
positive ([[def-qc-completely-positive-map]]) and trace-preserving, meaning

$$\operatorname{tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{tr}(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H),$$

where trace is the basis-independent trace of a finite-dimensional
endomorphism ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]). Trace preservation is
required on the full operator space, not only on density operators. This
definition is mathematical and assumes no physical realization.
Every quantum channel $\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ between nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces has $\|\Phi\|_\diamond=1$.

derivations.claim: Put $a=\|\Phi_1\|_\diamond$ and $b=\|\Phi_2\|_\diamond$. For any finite ancilla $R$, let $S_{\rm mid}:K_1\otimes H_2\otimes R\to H_2\otimes K_1\otimes R$ and $S_{\rm out}:K_2\otimes K_1\otimes R\to K_1\otimes K_2\otimes R$ be the wire swaps from [L3]. For each product matrix unit $X=X_1\otimes X_2\otimes X_R$ on $H_1\otimes H_2\otimes R$, factorwise tensor-map composition [L5] shows that first applying $\Phi_1\otimes\operatorname{id}_{H_2\otimes R}$, conjugating by $S_{\rm mid}$, applying $\Phi_2\otimes\operatorname{id}_{K_1\otimes R}$, and conjugating by $S_{\rm out}$ gives $\Phi_1(X_1)\otimes\Phi_2(X_2)\otimes X_R$. This is exactly $(\Phi_1\otimes\Phi_2\otimes\operatorname{id}_R)(X)$. By the matrix-unit basis [L7], equality holds for every operator $X$. The two amplified maps have induced trace norms at most $a$ and $b$; conjugating by the wire swaps preserves trace norm by [L3]. Hence the composite output has trace norm at most $ab\|X\|_1$, and taking the suprema proves $\|\Phi_1\otimes\Phi_2\|_\diamond\le ab$.

By [L1], choose unit rank-one operators $X_i=R_{x_i,y_i}$ on an ancilla of dimension $\dim H_i$ attaining $\|\Phi_i\|_\diamond$. The tensor input $X_1\otimes X_2$ has trace norm $\|X_1\|_1\|X_2\|_1=1$ by [L2]. After the factor reordering, its output is $\Phi_1(X_1)\otimes\Phi_2(X_2)$ by [L5] and [L7]; its trace norm is the product of the two output trace norms by [L2]. It is therefore an admissible test showing $\|\Phi_1\otimes\Phi_2\|_\diamond\ge ab$. Together with step 1.1 this proves multiplicativity.

Use the exact identity $$\Phi_1\otimes\Phi_2-\Psi_1\otimes\Psi_2=(\Phi_1-\Psi_1)\otimes\Phi_2+\Psi_1\otimes(\Phi_2-\Psi_2).$$ For each ancilla, [F1] gives the triangle inequality for the amplified trace norm; taking its supremum gives the diamond-norm triangle inequality. By [F2] the four factor maps are channels, so step 2.1 bounds the two tensor terms by $\|\Phi_1-\Psi_1\|_\diamond\|\Phi_2\|_\diamond$ and $\|\Psi_1\|_\diamond\|\Phi_2-\Psi_2\|_\diamond$. Both channel norms equal one by [L6], giving the stated sum.

For finite-dimensional density operators $\rho,\sigma$,
$$0\le F(\rho,\sigma)\le1,\qquad F(\rho,\sigma)=1\iff\rho=\sigma,\qquad F(\rho,\sigma)=0\iff\operatorname{supp}\rho\perp\operatorname{supp}\sigma.$$
For density operators $\rho,\sigma$ on $H$ and $\tau,\omega$ on $K$,
$$F(\rho\otimes\tau,\sigma\otimes\omega)=F(\rho,\sigma)F(\tau,\omega).$$

Let $H$ and $K$ be finite-dimensional (have finite bases by [[def-dimension]])
complex inner-product spaces. A
**quantum channel** from $H$ to $K$ is a complex-linear map
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ ([[def-linear-map]]) that is completely
positive ([[def-qc-completely-positive-map]]) and trace-preserving, meaning

$$\operatorname{tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{tr}(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H),$$

where trace is the basis-independent trace of a finite-dimensional
endomorphism ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]). Trace preservation is

derivations.claim: Apply data processing [L1] to the channel and the two inputs, then use its exact outputs and the tensor-product formula [L2]: $$F(\rho_0,\rho_1)\le F(\rho_0\otimes\rho_0,\rho_1\otimes\rho_1)=F(\rho_0,\rho_1)^2.$$ Writing $f=F(\rho_0,\rho_1)\in[0,1]$, the inequality $f\le f^2$ forces $f=0$ or $f=1$, because $f(1-f)\le0$ and both factors are nonnegative.
If $f=1$, [L2] gives $\rho_0=\rho_1$. If $f=0$, [L2] gives orthogonality of their supports. These are the asserted alternatives.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, let $\mathcal D(H)$ be its density operators (nonnegative operators of trace one; [[def-qc-density-operator]]), and let $S\subseteq\mathcal D(H)$ be any set, finite or infinite. A **broadcaster** for $S$ is one quantum channel $B:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(H\otimes H)$ (completely positive and trace-preserving; [[def-qc-quantum-channel]]) such that for every $\rho\in S$,
$$\operatorname{Tr}_1(B(\rho))=\rho\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{Tr}_2(B(\rho))=\rho.$$
Here $\operatorname{Tr}_1$ and $\operatorname{Tr}_2$ are the partial traces over the indicated output factors ([[def-qc-partial-trace]]). The joint output may be correlated; this definition does not require $B(\rho)=\rho\otimes\rho$.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

Let $H,K,E$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and let
$V:H\to K\otimes E$ be a linear isometry. Then
$$\Phi(X)=\operatorname{Tr}_E(VXV^\dagger),\qquad X\in\mathcal L(H),$$
is a quantum channel from $H$ to $K$.

For states $\rho,\sigma$ on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space $H$, let a finite POVM be a finite family $(E_a)_{a=1}^n$ of nonnegative operators summing to $I_H$. Then
$$F(\rho,\sigma)=\min_{(E_a)}\sum_{a=1}^n\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a)\operatorname{tr}(\sigma E_a)}.$$
The minimum is attained by a projective measurement with $d=\dim H$ rank-one outcomes.

For every finite-dimensional channel $\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ and states $\rho,\sigma\in\mathcal D(H)$,
$$F(\rho,\sigma)\le F(\Phi(\rho),\Phi(\sigma)).$$
No general equality characterization is asserted.

Let $T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product space. Then there exist a non-negative endomorphism $U$ and a linear
isometry $S:V\to V$ such that

$$T=SU\qquad\text{and}\qquad U=\sqrt{T^*T}.$$

Equivalently, $S$ is an isometry on $(\ker T)^\perp=\operatorname{im}U$. The
factor $S$ is unique if and only if $T$ is invertible.

For every linear map $A:H\to K$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces,

$$\|A\|_1=\operatorname{tr}_H\!\left(\sqrt{A^*A}\right).$$

Here $A^*A$ and its non-negative square root are endomorphisms of the domain
$H$; the trace is taken on $H$.

Let $A:H\to K$ be a linear map ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional complex
inner-product spaces. Then

$$\|A\|_1=\max\{\,|\operatorname{tr}_H(B^*A)|: B:H\to K\text{ linear and }\|B\|\le1\,\}.$$

Consequently, on the vector space of linear maps $H\to K$, the trace norm is
nonnegative, absolutely homogeneous, definite, and satisfies the triangle
inequality.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and let
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ have a finite Kraus representation
$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a\in A}K_a X K_a^\dagger$. Then $\Phi$ is completely positive.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and let
$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a\in A}K_aXK_a^\dagger$ be a finite Kraus representation,
where each $K_a:H\to K$. The map $\Phi$ is trace-preserving on all of
$\mathcal L(H)$, meaning $\operatorname{tr}_K(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{tr}_H(X)$
for every $X\in\mathcal L(H)$, if and only if
$$\sum_{a\in A}K_a^\dagger K_a=I_H.$$

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

derivations.claim: Since $\rho_0,\rho_1$ are faithful, the measurement-minimum theorem [L2] supplies a rank-one PVM $(E_b)$ whose classical overlap is $F(\rho_0,\rho_1)$. Every $p_{s,b}=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_sE_b)$ is positive: if $E_b=|b\rangle\langle b|$ and $\rho_s$ is positive definite, then $p_{s,b}=\langle\rho_sb,b\rangle>0$.

Put $\widetilde\rho_s=B(\rho_s)$. Data processing under $B$ gives $F(\rho_0,\rho_1)\le F(\widetilde\rho_0,\widetilde\rho_1)$. Data processing under either partial trace, whose outputs are $\rho_s$ by [L1], gives the reverse inequality. Hence equality holds. Measuring $E_b\otimes I$ on the first output factor, or $I\otimes E_b$ on the second, produces the same probabilities as measuring $E_b$ on the input; each classical overlap is $F(\widetilde\rho_0,\widetilde\rho_1)$ and so is optimal by [L2].

For any two states $R,S$ and a finite POVM $(Q_b)$ attaining the minimum overlap, choose a polar unitary $U$ with $U\sqrt R\sqrt S=\sqrt{\sqrt S R\sqrt S}$. For each outcome let $A_b=U\sqrt R Q_b^{1/2}$ and $C_b=\sqrt S Q_b^{1/2}$. The Hilbert–Schmidt norms satisfy $\|A_b\|_2^2=\operatorname{tr}(RQ_b)$ and $\|C_b\|_2^2=\operatorname{tr}(SQ_b)$, while their inner product is $\operatorname{tr}(U\sqrt R Q_b\sqrt S)$. Thus Cauchy–Schwarz and the triangle inequality give $$\sum_b\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}(RQ_b)\operatorname{tr}(SQ_b)}\ge\sum_b|\operatorname{tr}(U\sqrt R\,Q_b\sqrt S)|\ge|\operatorname{tr}(U\sqrt R\sqrt S)|=F(R,S).$$ Equality of the endpoints forces equality term by term in Cauchy–Schwarz and common nonnegative phase in the triangle inequality. For each outcome with $\operatorname{tr}(SQ_b)>0$, this gives a scalar $\gamma_b\ge0$ with $U\sqrt R\,Q_b^{1/2}=\gamma_b\sqrt S\,Q_b^{1/2}$. Applying this to the two optimal PVMs of step 2.1, there are unitaries $U,V$ and nonnegative $\alpha_b,\beta_b$ such that $$U\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_0}(I\otimes E_b)=\alpha_b\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_1}(I\otimes E_b),\quad V\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_0}(E_b\otimes I)=\beta_b\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_1}(E_b\otimes I),$$ and both $U,V$ satisfy $U\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_0}\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_1}=V\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_0}\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_1}=\sqrt{\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_1}\widetilde\rho_0\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_1}}$. For these two PVMs every outcome probability is positive by step 1.1 and the broadcaster marginals, so neither Cauchy–Schwarz vector is zero; dependence therefore gives the displayed scalar equations.

Set $G=\sum_b\alpha_bE_b$ and $J=\sum_b\beta_bE_b$. Summing the equations in step 3.1 gives $U\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_0}=\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_1}(I\otimes G)$ and $V\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_0}=\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_1}(J\otimes I)$. Multiply the first by $\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_0}U^*$ on the left and trace out the first factor; multiply the second by $\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_0}V^*$ and trace out the second. The marginal identities yield $\rho_0=A G=CJ$, where $A=\operatorname{Tr}_1(\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_0}U^*\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_1})$ and $C=\operatorname{Tr}_2(\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_0}V^*\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_1})$. Since $\rho_0$ is invertible, both $G$ and $J$ are invertible.

Left-multiply the two summed equations of step 4.1 by $\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_1}$ and trace out the first factor in the first equation and the second in the second. The partial-trace adjoint identity and the local-factor multiplication rule in [L1] give $A^*=\rho_1G$ and $C^*=\rho_1J$. Taking adjoints in $\rho_0=AG=CJ$ gives $\rho_0=G\rho_1G=J\rho_1J$. For either positive operator $G$ or $J$, conjugating this equation by $\rho_1^{1/2}$ shows $(\rho_1^{1/2}G\rho_1^{1/2})^2=\rho_1^{1/2}\rho_0\rho_1^{1/2}$, and likewise for $J$. Uniqueness of the positive square root [L4] therefore yields $G=J$.

The operators $G=J=\sum_b\alpha_bE_b$ are positive and invertible by step 4.1, so write $G|b\rangle=g_b|b\rangle$ with each $g_b>0$. Substituting $G=J$ into step 4.1 and eliminating $\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_1}$ gives $$V^*U\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_0}=\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_0}(G^{-1}\otimes G).$$ For $w=\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_0}(|b\rangle\otimes|c\rangle)\ne0$, this equation says the unitary $V^*U$ has eigenvalue $g_c/g_b>0$ on $w$, whose modulus must be one. Hence $g_b=g_c$; when they differ, $w=0$.

For any $b,b'$ with $g_b\ne g_{b'}$ and any $c$, either $g_c\ne g_b$, in which case step 5.2 gives $\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_0}|b,c\rangle=0$, or $g_c=g_b$, in which case it gives $\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_0}|b',c\rangle=0$. In the first case the column of $\widetilde\rho_0$ vanishes; in the second its corresponding row vanishes because $\sqrt{\widetilde\rho_0}$ is self-adjoint. Therefore every summand in $\langle b'|\rho_0|b\rangle=\sum_c\langle b',c|\widetilde\rho_0|b,c\rangle$ is zero. Thus $[G,\rho_0]=0$. Since $\rho_0=G\rho_1G$ from step 5.1, $\rho_1=G^{-1}\rho_0G^{-1}$ also commutes with $\rho_0$.

Conversely, diagonalize $\rho_0$ in an orthonormal basis by [L6]. Commutation makes each eigenspace invariant under $\rho_1$; the restriction of the self-adjoint $\rho_1$ to each eigenspace has an orthonormal eigenbasis by [L6]. Combining them gives a common orthonormal eigenbasis $(|j\rangle)$. Define $K_j=|j,j\rangle\langle j|$ and $B(X)=\sum_jK_jXK_j^*$. By [L7], $K_j^*K_j=|j\rangle\langle j|$, so the basis identity gives $\sum_jK_j^*K_j=I$; [L6] therefore makes $B$ completely positive and trace-preserving, hence a channel. For either diagonal state $\rho_s=\sum_j\lambda_{s,j}|j\rangle\langle j|$, $B(\rho_s)=\sum_j\lambda_{s,j}|j,j\rangle\langle j,j|$, whose two marginals are both $\rho_s$. This proves the reverse direction.

A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).
